crypto_audit.score_cap: Broken signature or key on the site certificate
crypto_audit.unreadable: Unreadable certificate: the chain sent by the server could not be analysed
finding.crypto_audit.chain_expired: The intermediate certificate "{subject}" expired {days} day(s) ago.
finding.crypto_audit.chain_expiring: The intermediate certificate "{subject}" expires in {days} day(s).
finding.crypto_audit.incomplete_chain: The server does not send all intermediate certificates: some clients (applications, older systems) will refuse the connection.
finding.crypto_audit.no_san: The certificate has no subject alternative names (SAN) extension: modern browsers reject it.
finding.crypto_audit.no_sct: No SCT (Certificate Transparency) is embedded in the certificate; the server may provide it another way, otherwise browsers reject it.
finding.crypto_audit.no_server_auth: The certificate is not intended for server authentication (extended key usage).
finding.crypto_audit.validity_too_long: The certificate is valid for {days} days, beyond the {limit}-day limit set by the CA/Browser Forum at its issuance date.
finding.crypto_audit.weak_key: The certificate "{subject}" uses a key that is too weak ({key_type} {bits} bits).
finding.crypto_audit.weak_signature: The certificate "{subject}" is signed with the obsolete {algorithm} algorithm.
module.crypto_audit.checks: Analyses the certificate chain sent by the server: signature algorithms (SHA-1, MD5), key size and type, validity period against the current CA/Browser Forum schedule, expired intermediates, complete chain, subject alternative names (SAN), server usage, SCTs (Certificate Transparency) and validation type (DV, OV, EV).
module.crypto_audit.fix:
Fix it at the source: almost all of these issues come from the certificate itself or its chain, not from a server setting. Ask the authority for a new certificate rather than changing the configuration.
If the signature is SHA-1 or MD5, or the key is too weak (RSA under 2048 bits, elliptic curve under 256 bits): create a new private key, ECDSA P-256 or RSA 3072 bits (`-newkey rsa:3072`), and a certificate signing request (CSR) with the command in the OpenSSL snippet, then submit it to the authority, which will sign it with SHA-256 or better.
If the issue concerns an intermediate certificate and not the site's own (weak signature or key, expired or soon-to-expire intermediate): it comes from the authority. Fetch its current chain (or have the certificate reissued, which supplies it) and replace the server's old intermediates file. If the authority keeps an obsolete algorithm, change authority.
If the subject alternative names (SAN) or the "server authentication" usage are missing: redo the request listing every site name in the SAN (`DNS:example.com`, `DNS:www.example.com`) and pick a TLS/SSL server certificate, not a code-signing, email or client certificate.
If the chain is incomplete: install the file that holds the site certificate followed by the intermediates, in that order (`fullchain.pem`, or the certificate concatenated with the authority's bundle), instead of the certificate alone. The root is not needed.
If the validity period exceeds the limit: reissue a certificate with the allowed lifetime (the CA/Browser Forum sets 200 days for certificates issued since 15 March 2026, 100 days from 15 March 2027, 47 days from 15 March 2029) and automate renewal with ACME.
If no SCT (Certificate Transparency) is found: reissue the certificate from a public authority, which embeds it automatically, or configure the server to attach the SCTs to the handshake. Browsers reject a certificate without SCTs.
Install the new certificate with its chain (see the nginx or Apache snippet), reload the server, then check: `openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -showcerts` must show the full chain; `openssl x509 -noout -text` on each certificate saved to a file shows the signature algorithm, key size and alternative names.
module.crypto_audit.fix_snippet:
# OpenSSL
openssl req -new -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:prime256v1 -nodes -keyout example.com.key -out example.com.csr -subj "/CN=example.com" -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:example.com,DNS:www.example.com"
openssl req -in example.com.csr -noout -text

# nginx
ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/example.com/fullchain.pem;
ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/example.com/privkey.pem;

# Apache
SSLCertificateFile    /etc/ssl/example.com/fullchain.pem
SSLCertificateKeyFile /etc/ssl/example.com/privkey.pem
module.crypto_audit.title: Certificate cryptographic audit
module.crypto_audit.why: A SHA-1 signature, a short key or a missing intermediate makes some clients reject the certificate or lets it be forged, even when the browser shows a padlock.
